Figure 17:Formality, text→\toimage.Rows: a person at a desk, a basket of laundry,
one person pouring water for another, a pair of shoes, a menu. None of the prompts mentions
clothing or register. Toward formal: suits, documents, neatly stacked laundry, dress shoes, a
plain typeset menu. Toward colloquial the scenes become warmer and more cluttered, and beyond−0.6-0.6they start to look like illustrations; beyond+0.6+0.6they wash out.

Figure 18:English vs. French, text→\toimage.Rows: a house, a town square, the
front page of a newspaper, a poster. Toward French: a mansard roof, a Beaux-Arts square,
mastheads and posters in French-looking but invented words. Toward English: vinyl siding and a
garage, plain paving, English headlines and slogans.

Figure 19:The same direction on everyday objects.Rows: a breakfast, a parked car, a
street sign, a station platform, a small shop. At+0.4+0.4the objects are French while the image
is still photographic (pastries, a vintage car, an enamel street sign, an iron station canopy,
a Haussmann shopfront); at+0.8+0.8the images turn golden and painterly.

Figure 20:Camera height, image→\toimage.Rows: a statue, an apartment tower, a
staircase, a person. Toward one pole the camera rises until it looks straight down on the
subject; toward the other it drops to near ground level. The subject stays the same.

Figure 21:Motion blur, image→\toimage.Rows: a cyclist, a dog, a train, a sports
car. Toward blurred, the background first streaks as in a panning shot while the subject stays
readable, then the whole frame blurs. Toward sharp, the scene fills with extra detail.

Figure 22:Resolution, image→\toimage.Rows: a breakfast, a bicycle, a postbox, a
poster, a living room. Toward high resolution scenes gain detail and clutter; toward low
resolution they first become simpler and emptier, then turn into pixel blocks, and collapse
at+0.8+0.8.
